after: ## How water and wind remove soil
alt: Left: on a bare slope, raindrops knock soil loose, run-off carries the particles downhill faster on steeper ground, and channels deepen into gullies. Right: on flat, open land with dry, loose, fine soil, strong wind lifts the finest particles, including much of the organic matter, leaving coarser, less fertile soil. Both happen where soil is unprotected by plants.
caption: Water erodes by raindrop impact, run-off and gullies; wind lifts the finest, most fertile particles.

alt: Two river cross-sections. Before: a deep channel with clear water. After eroded soil arrives: silt fills the bottom of the channel, making it shallower and the water cloudy. As a result the river holds less water, so flooding is more likely; reservoirs store less water; and cloudy water blocks light, harming aquatic life.
caption: Silt makes channels shallower and water cloudier: more flooding, less storage, harm to aquatic life.

alt: A chain of impacts: soil erosion removes fertile topsoil, so crop yields fall; where people rely on local harvests this causes malnutrition and famine; people are then displaced to towns or other farmland, spreading the pressure elsewhere.
caption: Erosion → lower yield → malnutrition → displacement.

alt: Four problems matched to strategies. Steep slopes and water erosion: terracing, contour ploughing, bunds. Flat, dry, windy land: wind breaks, bunds, vegetation cover. Bare soil after harvest: maintain vegetation cover, mulch or crop residue. Weak soil structure after monoculture: add organic matter.
caption: Choose strategies that fit the slope, wind, cover and soil structure in the question.

alt: Benefits and limitations of five strategies. Terracing works on steep slopes but needs much labour and can collapse. Contour ploughing is cheap but weaker on very steep slopes or in heavy rain. Wind breaks give wood and habitat but take land and years to grow. Vegetation cover is cheap and effective but may compete for water. Organic matter improves fertility but is bulky and needs a supply.
caption: Each strategy has a cost: labour, land, water or supply.

after: ## Worked example 1: interpreting erosion plot data
alt: A bar chart of soil lost in one year from four plots on the same slope: bare soil ploughed up and down slope 12.0 kg per square metre, contour ploughed 5.4, terraced 1.8 and permanent grass 0.6. Contour ploughing cuts loss by 55% and grass by 95%; bare soil loses 20 times as much as grass.
caption: Grass cover cut soil loss by 95%, terracing came next, contour ploughing by 55%.
